name: Hair cloning
lead: Hair cloning, also called hair multiplication or follicle neogenesis, is a proposed regenerative approach to hair loss in which a small number of cells from healthy follicles, such as dermal papilla cells, are multiplied in the laboratory and then implanted into balding scalp to form new follicles. [1][2] It is aimed at overcoming the main limit of hair transplantation, a finite supply of donor hair.

As of the sources consulted, hair cloning remains experimental. Wikipedia describes the field as in its early stages, with parts of the process shown at small scale, mostly in animals, and no approved product. [2] Companies including Intercytex and Aderans ended their programmes, and Stemson Therapeutics closed in December 2024. [2]
infobox: Culture and implantation of follicle-inducing cells

paras: Proposed methods take dermal papilla cells or follicle stem cells from a small scalp sample, expand them in culture, and implant them where they are meant to induce new follicles through interaction with surrounding epithelial cells. [1] Newer lines of work use induced pluripotent stem cells made from patient cells, 3D cell aggregates and scaffolds. [1][3]

According to Wikipedia, Intercytex concluded in 2008 that it had not fully developed its therapy, and Aderans stopped funding its research in July 2013. [2] In 2012 University of Pennsylvania researchers reported that bald and non-bald scalp had similar stem cell numbers but depleted progenitor cells in bald areas. [2]

Reported later milestones include human-derived follicles grown in mice with inconsistent hair direction (2015), hair from iPSC-derived human skin implanted in mice (2016), mouse follicles grown from iPSC-derived cells aligned to a 3D-printed shaft (2019), and a February 2026 Riken and OrganTech report of engineered follicles that cycled for 68 days in mice. [2] A 2016 laboratory study generated induced pluripotent stem cells from human hair follicle keratinocytes as a potential source for follicle cloning. [3]
No studies found. Related work is laboratory and animal research, such as the iPSC study of follicle keratinocytes [3] and the mouse experiments described by Wikipedia. [2]

Wikipedia lists inconsistent hair direction, thin follicles in earlier methods, depleted progenitor cells in bald scalp, and cycling shown only in mice as open problems. [2] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, adds that results with related stem-cell injections are described as modest and inconsistent. [1]

timeline.event: Intercytex concludes its follicle therapy is not fully developed. [2]
University of Pennsylvania report on progenitor cell depletion in bald scalp. [2]
Aderans stops funding its hair cloning research. [2]
iPSC-derived human skin produces hair in mice; iPSC study from follicle keratinocytes published. [2][3]
Stemson Therapeutics and UCSD grow follicles in mice with iPSC-derived cells. [2]

card.summary: Multiplying follicle cells in a lab to grow unlimited hair is a long-promised idea that remains in animal and lab research.
card.note: No approved product; commercial programmes have closed.

quick.overview:
Hair cloning would take cells from healthy follicles, multiply them in culture, and implant them to make new hair follicles, avoiding the donor limits of transplantation.

Per Wikipedia, it is in early stages, with milestones in mice and several company programmes ended.
quick.mechanism: Follicle-inducing cells such as dermal papilla cells, or iPSC-derived cells, are expanded in the lab and implanted to interact with scalp epithelium and form follicles.
quick.risks: No approved treatment exists, so no human safety record is cited. Obstacles listed include inconsistent hair direction, thin follicles and cycling shown only in mice.
